To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the naive model will be preferred over complex models when the number of predictor variables is large or when the sample size is small.

1) the naive model will outperform the econometric model when the number of predictors is too high, or when the number or points used to estimate the parameters is too small, and 2) the number of points held out for validation has little effect on the decision of whether to use the naive model or the econometric model.
the naive model will outperform the econometric model when the number of predictor variables used is greater than the number of data points available to estimate the parameters of the model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to choose between a simple and complex model for market share forecasting, when the complex model is based on an econometric model with many variables.
the conditions under which the simple econometric model (naive model) will be superior to the complex model.
the question of whether it pays to go for complex econometric models when the objective is to predict market share.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the naive model should be used when there is not enough information to fit the econometric model, and that the econometric model should be used whenever the information is available.

the decision to use a simple or complex econometric model for market share prediction depends on the relative sizes of the estimation and validation sample sizes and on the relative number of predictor variables and observations used in the model.

the naive model will outperform the more complex econometric models when the latter are not well-specified, and that the decision between the two models is not greatly affected by the size of the validation sample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the econometric model should be used when there is enough data to estimate a model with the right number of parameters.
naive models are expected to perform better than econometric ones when the number of predictors is large and/or the number of observations is small.
the naive model should be used when the sample size is small and the number of parameters is large, or when the number is large and the sample size is large.
The main takeaway from our work is that
managers should not use econometric models for forecasting unless they are confident that their data set is not too small or that their model is not too complex.
, when the number of predictors in the model is small, the naive model will perform better.
the decision to use a naive or econometric market share model should not be taken in the abstract, but should be based on the characteristics of the data at hand.
